claims.claim: Irenaeus was the bishop of Lugdunum (Lyon) in Gaul in the late second century, born about AD 120‑140 and dying about AD 200‑203.
He was a disciple of the apostolic father Polycarp and heard Polycarp’s preaching in Smyrna when he was a child.
After the martyrdom of Bishop Pothinus in the persecution of 177 AD, Irenaeus succeeded him as bishop of Lyon.
The Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching is a second‑century manual for Christian converts that sets out the essential points of the apostolic message.
Irenaeus wrote the work as a letter to his brother Marcianus, urging him to walk in godliness and to preserve his faith.
Its purpose was to “show forth in brief the preaching of the truth for the confirmation of [Marcianus’s] faith” and to shame those who “inculcate falsehood.”
The treatise belongs to Irenaeus’s broader effort to combat Gnostic heresies by demonstrating the authentic apostolic preaching.
The original Greek text was lost for nearly two millennia and survived only in an Armenian manuscript discovered in 1904.

The work matters because it provides a concise statement of early Christian doctrine, offers a window into how the second‑century church taught converts, and serves as a tool for refuting heretical teachings.
